title: 6 Teacher Personality Traits That Make Classroom Management More Difficult
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues that classroom management difficulties often trace back not to strategy but to the personality a teacher brings into the room each day. He identifies six traits—impatience, quickness to anger, pessimism, irritability, oversensitivity to misbehavior, and being easily frustrated—that undermine rapport and provoke restlessness or defiance in students. Each trait is explained in terms of how it erodes trust, consistency, or likeability with a class. Linsin contends these tendencies can surface even in teachers who are calm elsewhere, simply because a room full of active students brings them out. He closes by recommending a short daily visualization routine, done with eyes closed before students arrive, in which the teacher mentally rehearses calm, confident, rapport-building responses to the school day ahead.
points: Name your own triggers: impatience, anger, pessimism, irritability, thin skin, and frustration each quietly sabotage rapport and consistency.
A single flash of anger can undo weeks of relationship-building with a class.
Pessimistic attitudes toward difficult students leak out through tone and body language even when unspoken.
Use a two-minute pre-class visualization routine to mentally rehearse the calm, poised version of yourself.
Consistency, not emotional reactivity, is what earns students' trust and cooperation.
quotes: Many teachers become different people the minute their students walk through the door. Sometimes this is a good thing—if being around students makes you brighten like a Broadway singer or become as preternaturally calm as a mountain lake.

Impatient teachers talk fast, move fast, and tend to either look the other way in the face of misbehavior, or react emotionally to it. They rush through lessons , gloss over instructions, and out of necessity have lower expectations for students.
Irritability (grouchiness, moodiness) communicates to students that they can’t trust you or depend on you. It creates resentment, confusion, and instability.
Frequent sighs, rolling eyes, red-faced lectures . Outward signs of frustration can cause enveloping, knife-cutting tension in your classroom.

The way you present yourself to your students has a monumental effect on classroom management—more so than most teachers realize. If you’re at all susceptible to one or more of the personality traits above, then you’ll be a more effective teacher if you get a handle on them.
